analysis.one_liner: Bars people convicted of misdemeanor stalking from buying or owning guns.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote: it sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from January 2019 until the Congress ended, despite 35 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add two groups to the federal list of people who cannot legally buy or possess guns: anyone convicted of a misdemeanor crime of stalking, and — under an expanded definition — current or former dating partners covered by existing domestic violence gun restrictions. Today those restrictions largely cover spouses, ex-spouses, and people who lived together, leaving many abusive dating partners and convicted stalkers legally armed. Anyone convicted would keep standard due-process protections: the conviction only counts if the person had a lawyer or knowingly gave one up, and had a jury trial or gave that up too.
analysis.who_benefits: Stalking victims and survivors of abuse by dating partners. Research consistently finds that stalkers and abusive dating partners with firearms pose a serious lethal risk to the people they target; this bill would make it a federal crime for such a person, once convicted, to buy or keep a gun. A smaller benefit flows to the general public through fewer gun transfers to people with stalking convictions.

how_it_helps.text: It adds a new category to federal gun prohibitions: a person 'convicted in any court of a misdemeanor crime of stalking' may not ship, transport, possess, or receive firearms or ammunition, and may not be sold or given one.

It expands the federal definition of 'intimate partner' — the trigger for the existing domestic violence gun ban — to include dating partners and 'any other person similarly situated to a spouse,' closing the so-called boyfriend loophole.

The bill builds in due-process safeguards: a stalking conviction only triggers the gun ban if the defendant had counsel or knowingly waived it, and, where a jury trial was available, had a jury or knowingly waived one. Expunged or pardoned convictions generally do not count.

analysis.who_pays: People convicted of misdemeanor stalking lose the legal right to buy or possess firearms, and gun sellers lose that slice of customers. Because the prohibition covers conduct that states classify as misdemeanor stalking, some people convicted of lower-level stalking offenses would lose gun rights they would keep under the existing felony-based rules.

drawbacks.text: State stalking statutes vary widely, so the bill would rely on state misdemeanor definitions of stalking — including some that reach harassing conduct short of violence — to take away a constitutional right. Critics of similar measures argue that sweeps too broadly.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that a gun ban triggered by a misdemeanor, rather than a felony, is a serious consequence, and that the bill's protections depend on state courts actually providing the counsel and jury-trial rights the bill requires before the ban applies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is targeted and concrete: people who have already been convicted of stalking an intimate partner would no longer be able to legally acquire guns, and survivors of abuse by dating partners would get the same protection spouses already have. The cost falls on a narrow group — people with stalking convictions — and the bill hedges it with explicit counsel and jury-trial requirements. The main design weakness is dependence on uneven state stalking definitions, which is a fair objection but not one the bill's safeguards leave unaddressed entirely.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Amy Klobuchar introduced the bill on January 15, 2019, with 31 original cosponsors, all Democrats or the chamber's Independent.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary the day it was introduced.
The cosponsor list grew to 35 — 34 Democrats and 1 Independent — but no Republican signed on at any point.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral; the last entry is the January 15, 2019 referral to Judiciary.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People convicted of misdemeanor stalking and abusive dating partners keep unrestricted access to firearms under federal law, and gun sellers keep those customers. No one else is measurably better off; the bill simply never moved.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 31 original cosponsors on the day of introduction.

for.name: Sen. Mazie Hirono and 34 Democratic and Independent senators
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, growing the list to 35, though no Republican joined.

against.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: The committee the bill was referred to never held a hearing or markup on it; the action history ends with the referral.

against.name: National Rifle Association
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation expanding federal gun prohibitions to dating partners and stalking convictions.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's lone Independent; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never advanced in the Republican-run committee.

industries.note: The bill removes a group of people — those convicted of misdemeanor stalking and, under the expanded definition, certain abusive dating partners — from the legal customer base for guns and ammunition. The industry's interest in unrestricted sales runs against the bill's protection for stalking victims, though the affected customer slice is narrow.
